Justifications of physical chastisement grounded in proverbs or scripture-based discipline framing become more common in coverage as tolerance rises (direction A).

Reporting on the legal implementation of anti-violence treaties and laws grows over time, with more articles describing enacted measures and their enforcement, signalling movement toward 'never justifiable' (direction B).

Early coverage frames spousal beating through male authority and private discipline, while later coverage frames it through refuges and protective services, indicating a move toward 'never justifiable' (direction B).

In survey and opinion-poll reporting, early results are described with categorical rejection language, while later results increasingly feature conditional acceptance such as provocation or circumstances, indicating movement toward 'always justifiable' (direction A).
Coverage of vigilante behavior and neighbor-on-neighbor confrontations rises over time, signaling falling willingness to trust those nearby (Direction A).
Within local community-life coverage, mentions of shared community resources increase over time, indicating rising neighborly trust (Direction B).
Coverage shifts from shared-resource language toward confrontational neighbor-conflict language, indicating declining trust (Direction A).
Within homeowners' association coverage, reporting moves from legal enforcement and fines toward volunteer and social activities, suggesting rising neighborly trust (Direction B).
Reports of police being called on neighbors for minor disputes become more frequent over time, reflecting growing wariness toward people nearby (Direction A).
Coverage of schemes where trusted insiders defraud members of their own community (affinity-based swindles) increases, which would indicate growing distrust of people one knows personally.
In neighborhood coverage, language of keeping distance and locking up gives way to language of looking out for one another, which would indicate rising trust in people one knows.
In family coverage, reunion and welcoming language increases, which would indicate rising trust in relatives and close acquaintances.
Warnings shift from in-person and known-contact dealings toward voice cloning and impersonation of relatives, which would indicate growing suspicion even of voices and identities people know.
In dating coverage, warnings about deception by people met through apps increase, which would indicate growing distrust of people one gets to know personally.
Coverage of confidence scams and con artists rises over the period, signalling a more wary public toward unfamiliar people.
Within crowdfunding and online giving, coverage of strangers donating to one another and of pay-it-forward gestures increases, pointing to more open trust toward unknown people.
Early coverage frames dealings with strangers as handshake-based and informal; later coverage frames them around formal verification and identity checks, indicating reduced trust in unknown people.

On public health messaging, early coverage describes officials as hoaxers or misinformation sources, while later coverage describes them as trusted messengers, reflecting rising trust in these previously unfamiliar authorities.
In coverage of dating apps, safety warnings about meeting unknown matches rise over time, reflecting a shift toward distrust of people met for the first time.
As the share of households using a non-English language at home grows, more respondents have a mother born abroad, so coverage of multilingual homes should rise toward Yes.
Growing dual-nationality arrangements mean more people report a foreign-born parent, so coverage of dual citizenship should increase under Direction A.

Public discussion shifted from enforcement language about aliens and registration toward language about youth and families with undocumented parents, consistent with more respondents having immigrant mothers (Direction A).

Within coverage of births and maternity care, mentions of births to foreign-born mothers should grow as the immigrant-mother share rises (Direction B reverses this, so Direction B predicts a decline).

In coverage of marriage and intermarriage, early references to marrying across national origin lines give way to references to native-born spouses and grandchildren, tracking a shift toward No under Direction B.
Coverage of Anglo-Protestant and early-settler heritage declines over time, so references to such ancestry should fall if the share answering that a father is native-born rises.
Among coverage of Latino and Asian American communities, references to parents who emigrated from specific countries should rise if the share of immigrant fathers grows.
Framing shifts from multigenerational farming or pioneer ancestry toward recent arrival and immigrant roots, which would indicate movement toward Yes.
